## Background 

Today, we will explore some core machine learning methods that are very popular in bioinformatics. THese include **clustering** and **dimensionallity reduction**. 

## K-means 

The main function in "base R" from K-means clustering is called `k-means()`

Before we go too deep, let's make up some "simple" data that we can cluster and know if we are getting good results or not. To do this we can use the `rnorm()` function: 

```{r}
#tells us how many things we wanna get back AKA output 
rnorm(10)
```

```{r}
hist(rnorm(100000))
```

Give me 30 points centered at +3 and a second set with a mean of +3
```{r}
tmp <- c( rnorm(30, mean = -3), rnorm(30, mean=+3) )
x <- cbind(tmp, rev(tmp))
x
```
```{r}
plot(x)
```

Now Try `kmeans()` on this input data `x`

```{r}
# components tell you how to get results of this cluster 
k <- kmeans(x, centers = 2)
k
```

To get to the results we can use `k$size` etc. to access each component result: 

>Q. How many points are in each cluster? 

```{r}
k$size
```

>Q. What "component" of your results object details cluster membership? 

```{r}
k$cluster
```

>Q. What "component" of your results object details cluster centers?

```{r}
k$centers
```

>Q. Make a results figure of our data with points colored by cluster along with cluster centers? 

```{r}
plot(x, col = c(1,2) ) 
```

```{r}
plot(x, col = k$cluster) 
points(k$centers, col="blue", pch=15)
```

>Q. Run kmeans again and cluster into 4 clusters producing a resuls figure with points colored by cluster and showing the cluster centers? 

```{r}
k4<- kmeans(x, centers = 4)
k4
k4$cluster
k4$centers
plot(x, col = k4$cluster)
points(k$centers, col="blue", pch=15)
```

> **N.B.** You need to tell K-means the number of clusters (i.e. selt `centers=2`)!! 

One approach is to try different values for `centers` and then pick the best one:

```{r}
ans <- NULL 

for(i in 1:10) {
  cat(i, "\n")
km<- kmeans(x, centers = i)
ans <- c(ans,km$tot.withinss)
}
```

```{r}
plot(ans, type="o", 
     xlab="Number of Clusters", 
     ylab="Total Sum of Square Distance")
```

## Hierarchical Clustering 

The main function in "base" R for is called `hclust()`
```{r}
# hclust()
```

This function does not take your "raw" data for clustering. You must first build a "distance matrix" from your data and pass this as input for `hclust()`. 


```{r}
d <- dist(x)
hc <- hclust(d)
hc 
#hclust()
```

```{r}
plot(hc)
#one side of dendogram is below 30 while another side is above 30 
# main thing we look at is the crossbars 
abline(h=8, col="red")
```

Once we have our `hclust` object (our "tree" or "cluster dendrogram") we can "cut" the tree to reveal the clustering pattern: 
```{r}
cutree(hc, h=8)
```

You can use either `h=` or `k=` arguments to `cutree()`

```{r}
cutree(hc, k=4)
```

>Q. Make a plot of input data `x` with my clusters from `hclust()` (i.e colored by cluster membership from cutting the tree)

```{r}
grps <- cutree(hc, h=8)
plot(x, col = grps)
points(grps, col="blue", pch=15)
```

## Principle Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is a dimensionality reduction method that is popular for revealing patterns in complex data sets. 

### Analysis of UK Food Data 

Let's look at some data on eating habits of folks from the UK to see if there are patterns and trends that have some regions being distinct from others. 

### Data Import 

This data is made available in CSV format so we can use `read.csv()`: 

```{r}
url <- "https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods"
x <- read.csv(url, row.names=1)
x
```
>Q1. How many rows and columns are in your new data frame named x? What R functions could you use to answer this questions?

```{r}
nrow(x)
ncol(x)
```

>Q2. Which approach to solving the ‘row-names problem’ mentioned above do you prefer and why? Is one approach more robust than another under certain circumstances?
Some plots: HW 

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=T, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```

>Q3. Changing what optional argument in the above barplot() function results in the following plot?: 

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=F, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
#changing T to F 
```

>Q4. Changing what optional argument in the above ggplot() code results in a stacked barplot figure?:

```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

x_long <- x |>
  rownames_to_column("Food") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Food,
    names_to = "Country",
    values_to = "Consumption"
  )

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(x_long) +
  aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Pairs plots and heatmaps 

One plot that can be useful fo relatively small datasets is a `pairs()` plot. 

>Q5. We can use the pairs() function to generate all pairwise plots for our countries. Can you make sense of the following code and resulting figure? What does it mean if a given point lies on the diagonal for a given plot?

```{r}
pairs(x, col=rainbow(nrow(x)), pch=16)
```

>Q6.Based on the pairs and heatmap figures, which countries cluster together and what does this suggest about their food consumption patterns? Can you easily tell what the main differences between N. Ireland and the other countries of the UK in terms of this data-set?: HW 

Based on the pairs and heatmap figures, England and Wales cluter together, suggesting that these countries have similar food consumption habits! From the dataset, I can tell that Northern Ireland is the most different from other nations but it can be hard to know what foods contribute to its drastic differences! 

> **Key Point**: Even relatively small datasets can prove challenging to interpret 

Given that it is quite difficult to make sense of even this relatively small data set. Hopefully, we can clearly see that a powerful analytical method is absolutely necessary if we wish to observe trends and patterns in larger datasets.

## PCA to the rescue! 

The main function in "base" R for PCA is called `prcomp()`: 

This function will require the transpose of our dataset 

```{r}
pca<- prcomp( t(x) )
```

We can see how well our PCA results are doing in terms of the *variance captured* form the original data in each PC. 

```{r}
summary (pca)
```

I can see what is in my `pca` result object by: 

```{r}
attributes(pca)
```

Of these `pca$x` is our main result. We can use it to make a results figure often called a PCA plot (or score plot). 

```{r}
pca$x
```
```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(pca$x) + 
  aes(PC1, PC2) + 
  geom_point(col=c("orange", "red", "blue", "darkgreen"))
```

>Q7. Complete the code below to generate a plot of PC1 vs PC2. The second line adds text labels over the data points.: HW 

```{r}
# Create a data frame for plotting
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)

# Plot PC1 vs PC2 with ggplot
ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = rownames(pca$x)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw()
```
>Q8.  Customize your plot so that the colors of the country names match the colors in our UK and Ireland map and table at start of this document.

```{r}
country_colors <- c("England" = "orange",
  "Wales" = "red",
  "Scotland" = "blue",
  "N.Ireland" = "darkgreen"
)

ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = rownames(pca$x)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5,
            col = country_colors[rownames(pca$x)]) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw()
```
Now, we can calcuate how much variation in the original data each PC accounts for! 
```{r}
v <- round( pca$sdev^2/sum(pca$sdev^2) * 100 )
v
```

We can also examine the importance of each PC! 
```{r}
z <- summary(pca)
z$importance
```
These results can be summarized into a scree plot: 

```{r}
# Create scree plot with ggplot
variance_df <- data.frame(
  PC = factor(paste0("PC", 1:length(v)), levels = paste0("PC", 1:length(v))),
  Variance = v
)

ggplot(variance_df) +
  aes(x = PC, y = Variance) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  xlab("Principal Component") +
  ylab("Percent Variation") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0))

```

A "loadings" plot can show us how the original dimensions/variables contribute to our new PC axis. THis is detailed in the `pca$rotation` component of our result object: 
```{r}
pca$rotation
```

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) + 
  aes(PC1, row.names(pca$rotation))+ 
  geom_col()
```

Let's focus on PC1 loeading plots: 
```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(x = PC1, 
      y = reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC1)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  xlab("PC1 Loading Score") +
  ylab("") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

>Q9. Generate a similar ‘loadings plot’ for PC2. What two food groups feature prominantely and what does PC2 maninly tell us about?

```{r}
  ggplot(pca$rotation) +
aes(x = PC2, 
      y = reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC2)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  xlab("PC2 Loading Score") +
  ylab("") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

The main two groups that feature preominantely are fresh potatoes and soft drinks! This means that PC2 mainly shows differences in food consumption patterns between nations!
